newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end down on strong Dec job growth.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end down on strong Dec job growth.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended sharply lower on Friday after the government reported that U.S. payroll employment grew briskly in December.
The Labor Department reported that non-farm payrolls expanded by 262,000 jobs in December.
Economists, on average, had looked for growth approaching 200,000 jobs.
Another aspect of the labor report that unnerved a market focused on the inflationary implications of wage growth was a 0.5 percent increase in average hourly earnings.
Ward McCarthy, managing director of Stone & McCarthy Research Associates, said the sharp earnings rise would make the markets and policy makers nervous.
"It's going to resurrect concerns that labor market conditions are too tight," he said.

In the selling spurred by the employment report, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell nearly two full points, its yield rising as high as 6.90 percent, its highest level since closing at 6.92 percent on September 30.
The labor report aggravated concerns that the Federal Reserve might raise interest rates in the coming months.
In a Reuters poll, however, only a small minority of economists said they believed that the Fed would raise rates at its February 4-5 policy meeting.
"The Fed's on hold," said Neal Soss, chief economist at Credit Suisse First Boston.
Selling died down after the market had fallen to the lowest levels of the previous day's session, traders said.
After steadying at those sharply lower levels, some short-covering emerged in the futures pit in Chicago and in the cash market.
"Thursday's lows held as support and the market consolidated," said Greg Carr, analyst at A.G. Edwards & Sons.
The benchmark 30-year bond finished at 95-19/32, down 1-6/32 to yield 6.85 percent, versus Thursday's closing yield of 6.75 percent and Wednesday's closing yield of 6.84 percent.
"On the retail side, we saw good buying on dips," said Carr. "We saw aggressive buying of strips that were yielding seven percent. Investors were very much interested in that."
But Carr said the market remained "cautious" and "jittery" and worried about wage inflation.
Benning, too, minimized the importance of the late afternoon buying that erased the steepest of the market's losses.

"We were down a lot on the day so some guys took back some shorts, but it wasn't all that significant," said Joseph Benning, a trader at Daiwa Securities America Inc. "Rome wasn't destroyed in a day. It takes a while."
Benning said he would "not be the least bit surprised" to see the Fed tighten monetary policy in February.

Two-year notes ended at 99-15/32, down 6/32, yielding 6.04 percent. Five-year notes fell 16/32 to finish at 98-30/32, yielding 6.38 percent. Ten-year notes dropped 25/32 to end at 99-7/32, yielding 6.61 percent.

Three-month bill rates rose four basis points to finish at 5.03 percent. Six-month bill rates jumped five basis points to close at 5.12 percent. Year bill rates rose eight basis points to end at 5.34 percent.
-- North American Treasury Desk 212-859-1679
